item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #451
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

As the Renters’ Reform Act continues to reshape the UK rental market, landlords and tenants alike are navigating new challenges and changes. From rising demand for guarantors to delays in repossession cases, the landscape of renting is evolving rapidly. Here’s a closer look at the latest developments affecting the private rental sector.

Rising Demand for Guarantors

Since the introduction of the Renters’ Reform Act, which prohibits landlords from requesting multiple months’ rent in advance, there has been a noticeable increase in tenants being asked to provide a guarantor. According to Housing Hand, a leading tenant referencing company, 37% of renters are unaware of what a guarantor is or how the process works.

Graham Hayward, Managing Director at Housing Hand, highlights that landlords are seeking alternative forms of security. “With tenants no longer able to pay rent upfront, guarantors have become a key requirement for many landlords,” he explains. The company also reports that 37% of renters would be unsure of how to manage if they couldn’t pay their rent, while 33% admit to not planning their finances effectively for the future.

Rent Tribunals Favour Tenants

New analysis by LonRes reveals that rent tribunals are increasingly siding with tenants in disputes over rent increases. The average waiting time for a tribunal hearing is now 96 days nationwide, rising to 142 days in London. Of the 1,325 rent disputes recorded since January 2025, 73% were ruled in favour of tenants, with tribunals finding the proposed rent was too high. Only 18% of cases upheld the landlord’s suggested rent increase.

Chris Welch of LonRes emphasises the importance of landlords setting rent rises accurately and with solid evidence. “Tribunals will never set a higher rent than what the landlord has proposed. They will either lower it or keep it the same. This underscores the need for landlords to ensure their evidence is watertight before initiating a rent increase,” he advises.

Delays in Repossession Cases

The Renters’ Reform Act has also made it more challenging for landlords to regain possession of their properties. A survey by Goodlord found that 25% of landlords now find the process more difficult, with 39% becoming more cautious when vetting potential tenants. Additionally, 9% of landlords are spending more time trying to retain good tenants to avoid the complexities of repossessing a property.

Further research highlights the growing issue of fraudulent tenancy applications, with 41 out of every 1,000 applications flagged as suspicious. These delays and challenges are prompting landlords to rethink their strategies and prioritise thorough tenant checks.

As the rental market adapts to these regulatory changes, both landlords and tenants are encouraged to stay informed and seek professional guidance where necessary. With guarantor requirements, rent tribunals, and repossession delays shaping the sector, understanding these developments is crucial for navigating the evolving landscape of UK renting.

item.title: Record number of landlords taken to court over rent rises – legal experts react
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The number of rental disputes reaching property tribunals has reached unprecedented levels following the implementation of the Renters’ Rights Act. Recent data reveals tribunals made 166 market rent decisions in July alone – nearly four times the figure recorded during the same period last year. With 60% of cases initiated by tenants since the legislation came into force in May, these statistics highlight a dramatic shift in the rental market landscape.

How the Renters’ Rights Act has changed the landscape

The Renters’ Rights Act has fundamentally altered the dynamics between landlords and tenants by abolishing Section 21 'no-fault' evictions. Previously, tenants often hesitated to challenge rent increases due to fears of retaliatory eviction. The removal of this threat, coupled with changes to tribunal processes, appears to have emboldened renters to exercise their rights more freely.

Under the new rules, tenants who unsuccessfully challenge a rent increase only face higher payments from the tribunal decision date, rather than potentially owing backdated amounts. This reduced financial risk has contributed to the surge in cases, with monthly tribunal decisions more than doubling from the pre-legislation average of 42 to 129 in June and 166 in July.

What landlords need to know about rent increases

Legal experts emphasise that landlords must now provide comprehensive evidence to justify proposed rent increases. Simply citing rising costs is no longer sufficient – robust documentation including comparable local lettings, property condition reports, and recent rental transactions is essential.

  • Maintain detailed records of how the proposed rent figure was calculated
  • Follow the statutory Section 13 process precisely
  • Consider property-specific factors like location and amenities
  • Prepare to demonstrate market rent levels with concrete evidence

Property professionals suggest this shift towards evidence-based decision making may lead to more transparent and fairer rental pricing. However, it also places greater administrative responsibilities on landlords to maintain thorough documentation and follow correct procedures.

As the rental market continues to adapt to these legislative changes, both landlords and tenants may benefit from familiarising themselves with the new rules and their implications. With rent challenges becoming more common, understanding the tribunal process and evidence requirements could help prevent disputes before they arise.

item.title: UK property market isn’t broken – but something is definitely blocking it
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property market continues to show resilience, with buyer demand and housing supply remaining relatively stable. However, recent data suggests that many properties are struggling to progress from listing to completion. According to the latest Property Market Stats for week 33, covering the period ending 23 August, the market is facing challenges that may be slowing transactions. This raises questions about whether current conditions, unrealistic asking prices, or overvaluations are contributing to the issue.

Current Market Trends

In week 33, there were 31,800 new property listings, slightly down from 32,600 the previous week. This figure is below both the 2026 weekly average of 36,300 and the 10-year average for week 33 of 33,000. Year-to-date listings stand at 1.198 million, marginally lower than 2025’s figures but ahead of 2024 and the pre-pandemic 2017–2019 average. Meanwhile, 23,300 homes were sold subject to contract (STC) this week, down from 24,400 the previous week. This figure is also below the 10-year week 33 average of 25,100 and the 2026 weekly average of 24,500. Year-to-date sales STC are 7.2% lower than 2025 and slightly below 2024, though still above pre-pandemic levels.

The Impact of Price Reductions

Price reductions have become a notable feature of the current market, with 23,300 properties seeing price adjustments this week alone. This represents a significant portion of the 767,000 homes currently listed for sale across the UK. The prevalence of reductions suggests that some sellers may be setting initial asking prices too high, leading to longer marketing periods and a higher likelihood of fall-throughs. The data also highlights that the chance of selling decreases the longer a property remains on the market, emphasising the importance of realistic pricing from the outset.

Focus on the Bath Market

The analysis also delves into the Bath property market, comparing local estate agents based on their ability to convert instructions into successful sales rather than focusing solely on market share. This approach provides a more nuanced understanding of agent performance and could help sellers make informed decisions when choosing an agent. The findings underscore the value of selecting an estate agent with a strong track record in achieving completions, particularly in a market where transactions are taking longer to finalise.

While the UK property market remains robust, it is clear that certain factors are hindering the smooth progression of transactions. Homeowners may wish to consider setting realistic asking prices to avoid prolonged marketing periods and potential fall-throughs. Similarly, working with estate agents who have a proven ability to convert listings into sales could be beneficial in navigating the current market conditions.

item.title: Agency boss slams 300% second-home surcharge as housing ‘sticking plaster’
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Edinburgh’s proposed 300% council tax surcharge on second homes has sparked debate about whether the measure will meaningfully address the city’s housing challenges. Local letting agency DJ Alexander has criticised the policy as a "sticking plaster" solution that may fail to deliver promised benefits around affordability and housing supply.

Questionable impact on housing market

Under the council’s plans, owners of second properties and long-term vacant homes could see their council tax bills quadruple. A Band A property would attract an annual charge of £4,336, while Band H homeowners might face £15,935. The council estimates these premiums could generate £4m yearly, while encouraging owners to bring empty properties back into use.

However, critics highlight that Edinburgh’s 1,400 second homes represent just 0.5% of the city’s 265,000-property housing stock. With only 1,700 long-term empty properties, industry experts question whether targeting this small segment will meaningfully affect housing availability or affordability. The limited scale of the policy has led some to suggest its impact may be more symbolic than substantive.

Broader housing challenges persist

Housing campaigners note that Edinburgh faces deeper structural issues. During 2025-26, construction began on just 1,850 new homes - with only 539 being social housing. Meanwhile, the social housing waiting list reached 31,589 applicants last summer, with a third waiting over five years. Homelessness figures reveal 7,866 households (including 3,980 children) were without permanent accommodation in early 2025.

David Alexander of DJ Alexander Scotland commented: "This policy appears to address the housing emergency but is largely performative. The revenue raised is relatively low, it won’t substantially increase affordable homes, and is unlikely to reduce rents or prices as claimed." The agency suggests focusing on accelerating new builds and social housing delivery would prove more effective.

The proposal also raises questions about potential exemptions. Reports suggest MSPs requiring Edinburgh second homes due to distant constituencies may qualify for relief - a detail likely to fuel further debate about fairness and policy effectiveness.

As Edinburgh City Council prepares to vote on the surcharge, the discussion highlights the complex balancing act between generating revenue, discouraging property hoarding, and delivering meaningful solutions to the housing crisis. Homeowners affected by the changes may wish to review their financial planning, whilst housing advocates continue calling for more comprehensive supply-side solutions.

item.title: Renters now spending almost a third of income on rent as demand shifts
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals UK renters are now dedicating nearly a third of their income to housing costs, as rental prices continue to climb across most regions. The latest market analysis shows average monthly rents have reached £1,369 nationally, marking a 4.3% annual increase, with London maintaining its position as the most expensive rental market at £2,418 per month.

Changing rental landscape

The private rental sector is undergoing significant shifts, with both tenants and landlords adapting to new market conditions. The average UK renter is now 31.5 years old, though regional variations exist – Scotland's tenant population averages just 25 years old, reflecting its substantial student accommodation market.

Landlords appear to be adjusting their strategies in response to the Renters' Rights Act and the shift towards periodic tenancies. Rather than prioritising quick property occupancy, many are now focusing on securing longer-term tenants. This change comes as affordability pressures lead renters to seek more stable housing arrangements.

Regional hotspots emerge

While London continues to account for the highest volume of new tenancies, Kent has experienced remarkable growth with a 121% increase in rental agreements. The county's appeal stems from its transport links to the capital and demand for new-build properties, particularly family homes with two or three bedrooms. Average rents in Kent have risen by 5% year-on-year.

The North West and Yorkshire have also seen sustained rental growth, with prices increasing by 5% to £1,215 and £1,283 respectively. Demand has been particularly strong in towns between Liverpool and Manchester, where tenants are balancing affordability with access to employment hubs. Manchester's growing economic importance may further boost the regional market.

  • London average rent: £2,418/month
  • Kent tenancy agreements up 121%
  • North West rents increased by 5% to £1,215
  • Yorkshire rents rose 5% to £1,283

As rental costs consume an increasing proportion of household budgets, both tenants and landlords are adapting to a market where affordability and stability have become paramount considerations. The coming months may see further regional variations as economic factors and housing policies continue to shape the rental landscape.

item.title: Commuter-belt new-build demand three times that of London
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Demand for new-build properties in commuter towns has surged to three times the level seen in London, according to recent data. This trend highlights a significant shift in buyer preferences, with many opting for homes in areas offering more space and affordability whilst maintaining access to the capital. Limited supply and strong buyer interest are also pushing prices higher in these key commuter counties.

Why Are Commuter Towns So Popular?

Commuter towns have become increasingly attractive to buyers seeking a balance between urban convenience and suburban living. With remote and hybrid working arrangements now more common, many homeowners are prioritising larger properties with gardens over proximity to city centres. Towns such as Reading, Guildford, and Chelmsford are particularly sought after, offering excellent transport links to London alongside lower property prices compared to the capital.

Additionally, new-build developments in these areas often come with modern amenities and energy-efficient features, appealing to buyers looking for properties that require minimal upkeep. The appeal of a quieter lifestyle, coupled with access to good schools and local amenities, has further boosted demand in these regions.

Impact on Prices and Supply

The high demand for new-builds in commuter towns has led to a notable increase in property prices. Limited supply has exacerbated this trend, with developers struggling to keep pace with buyer interest. As a result, prices in some commuter counties have risen significantly, making it increasingly challenging for first-time buyers to enter the market.

For those considering purchasing a new-build in these areas, it could be worth exploring shared ownership schemes or government incentives such as the Help to Buy Equity Loan, which may help make homeownership more accessible. Additionally, working with a mortgage broker might help borrowers secure competitive rates tailored to their financial situation.

As demand for commuter-town properties continues to outstrip supply, homeowners and investors alike may wish to keep a close eye on market trends. With prices rising and competition intensifying, careful planning and research could prove essential for those looking to make the most of this growing market.

item.title: Searches up in every region for first time in year
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New data reveals that property searches have increased across all UK regions for the first time in twelve months, signalling renewed buyer interest despite ongoing market challenges. While mortgage rates remain elevated compared to recent years and completed sales volumes remain subdued, this uptick in activity suggests growing confidence among prospective homeowners.

Nationwide search growth signals market shift

Recent figures indicate a consistent rise in property searches throughout England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland – the first simultaneous increase recorded since summer 2023. This pattern emerges alongside reports of more stable house prices following the volatility seen earlier in the year. Mortgage advisers note that whilst affordability pressures persist, buyers appear to be adapting to the current lending landscape.

The resurgence spans all property types, with particular interest in three-bedroom family homes and smaller flats appealing to first-time buyers. Estate agents report that realistic pricing strategies from vendors may be contributing to this renewed engagement, as sellers adjust expectations to align with current market conditions.

Market challenges remain despite increased interest

Industry analysts caution that while search activity provides an encouraging indicator, several headwinds continue to affect the housing market. Mortgage approvals, whilst improving from their 2023 lows, remain below pre-pandemic levels. The average two-year fixed mortgage rate currently sits approximately 1.5 percentage points higher than the historic lows seen during the peak of ultra-low interest rates.

First-time buyers in particular face significant hurdles, with higher deposit requirements and stricter affordability assessments. However, some lenders have recently introduced more competitive products aimed at this demographic, including mortgages with higher loan-to-value ratios and longer initial fixed periods.

Regional variations in activity levels persist, with the strongest search growth reported in the North West and Wales. These areas continue to offer relatively better affordability compared to London and the South East, though all regions show positive momentum in buyer enquiries.

Looking ahead

Property professionals suggest this nationwide increase in searches could foreshadow a gradual market recovery, provided economic conditions remain stable. The Bank of England's future interest rate decisions will play a crucial role in determining whether this trend translates into sustained sales growth.

For those considering entering the market, mortgage brokers recommend obtaining an agreement in principle to strengthen negotiating positions. Whilst challenges remain, this data suggests cautious optimism may be returning to the UK property market after a prolonged period of uncertainty.

item.title: Repossession challenges for 1 in 4 landlords
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research reveals that a quarter of UK landlords are facing significant difficulties when attempting to repossess properties, with many reporting increasingly complex legal processes and rising operational costs. The findings highlight growing challenges in the private rental sector that could influence investment decisions for buy-to-let property owners.

Legal hurdles in the repossession process

Landlords across England and Wales are encountering more stringent requirements when seeking to regain possession of their properties. The Section 8 and Section 21 notice processes have become notably more complex following recent legislative changes. Many property owners report delays of several months before cases reach court, with some describing the system as "overburdened".

Key challenges include:

  • Stricter evidence requirements for possession claims
  • Extended notice periods in many circumstances
  • Increased scrutiny of landlord compliance with regulations
  • Higher legal costs associated with repossession cases

Rising costs and compliance pressures

Alongside repossession difficulties, landlords are facing mounting financial pressures from compliance requirements. item.title: Alarm bells for surveying sector as half prepare to retire
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s residential surveying sector is facing a potential crisis, with nearly half of its workforce planning to retire within the next decade. Research conducted by Skyline, as part of its Surveyor Live programme, reveals that 46% of surveyors do not expect to remain in the profession by 2033. This alarming statistic highlights the urgent need to attract younger talent to the industry.

An Ageing Workforce

The survey, which gathered responses from independent residential surveyors, paints a concerning picture of the sector’s demographics. Over 62% of respondents were aged 50 or older, whilst fewer than 16% were under 40. This ageing workforce suggests that the industry could soon face a significant shortage of experienced professionals if efforts to recruit and train younger surveyors are not prioritised.

Alan Milstein, Director at Skyline, emphasised the importance of understanding the sector’s workforce dynamics. “As an industry, surveying lacks reliable data about the demographics and structure of our community. We felt a responsibility to better understand the people who provide such vital services to the property industry,” he said.

Traditional Practices and Technological Hesitance

The research also sheds light on how surveyors currently operate and their attitudes towards technology. Quality remains the top priority for 66.4% of respondents, with many preferring traditional methods such as cameras and paper over digital tools like apps and tablets. This focus on quality over volume reflects the sector’s commitment to maintaining high standards in property assessments.

When it comes to artificial intelligence (AI), opinions are divided. While most surveyors acknowledge that AI could simplify their work, 54% expressed reluctance to integrate the technology more deeply into their businesses. This cautious approach suggests that the industry may need time to adapt to technological advancements.

The Need for Greater Engagement

With such a high proportion of surveyors nearing retirement, the sector must act swiftly to address its looming workforce challenge. Greater engagement with schools, colleges, and universities could help raise awareness of surveying as a viable and rewarding career path. Encouraging younger generations to join the profession will be essential to ensuring its sustainability.

Skyline plans to conduct this survey annually, tracking changes in demographics, working practices, and technology adoption over time. This data will be invaluable in assessing whether the profession has the capacity to handle proposed changes to the homebuying process, such as mandatory upfront condition reports.

The findings underscore the importance of preparing the surveying sector for the future. Without a concerted effort to attract and retain younger talent, the industry risks losing the expertise needed to support the UK’s property market.

item.title: Spicerhaart makes £1.7m tech bet as lettings regulation intensifies
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Estate agency group Spicerhaart has committed £1.7 million to develop custom property management technology, aiming to streamline compliance processes for landlords navigating an increasingly regulated rental market. The bespoke platform, created in collaboration with proptech specialist Rex Software, represents a five-year investment designed to help property managers stay ahead of legislative changes like those introduced in the Renters' Rights Act 2025.

Tailored technology for complex compliance

Rather than adopting an off-the-shelf solution, Spicerhaart partnered with Rex Software to build a system specifically around its lettings operations. The platform draws on the agency's experience handling hundreds of thousands of tenancies, addressing common challenges around regulatory adherence, maintenance coordination and tenant communications.

Key features of the new system include automated tracking of safety certificates, scheduled property inspections and renewal reminders. The technology aims to reduce administrative burdens while providing property managers with real-time oversight of compliance across Spicerhaart's portfolio. Early identification of potential issues could help landlords avoid costly penalties for missed regulatory requirements.

Supporting landlords through regulatory change

The investment coincides with Spicerhaart's establishment of a new Compliance and Pre-Tenancy Centre of Excellence, providing specialist support to its 200-strong property management team. As rental regulations become more complex, landlords may find value in working with agencies that prioritise compliance infrastructure.

Kelly-Anne Flynn, Managing Director of Property Management and Lettings Operations at Spicerhaart, noted: "The regulatory landscape has changed significantly, and landlords naturally seek clarity about their obligations. Our new system provides greater assurance that properties remain compliant as legislation evolves."

The growing role of proptech in lettings

This substantial investment reflects the increasing importance of technology in the rental sector, particularly as agencies balance growing compliance demands with the need to maintain service quality. Automated systems that handle documentation and deadline management could prove particularly valuable for landlords managing multiple properties or those less familiar with recent regulatory changes.

While the £1.7 million commitment represents a significant outlay, it demonstrates how forward-thinking lettings agencies are adapting their operations to protect both landlords and tenants in a rapidly changing market. Property investors might consider an agency's technological capabilities alongside traditional factors when selecting a management partner.

As regulation continues to intensify across the private rental sector, such investments in compliance technology may become increasingly common as agencies seek to provide landlords with greater peace of mind while maintaining operational efficiency.

item.title: One part of the mortgage market is growing fast
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The later life mortgage market has seen significant growth in the second quarter of 2026, according to the latest figures from UK Finance. The data reveals a 13.4% year-on-year increase in the number of new loans advanced to older borrowers, totalling 37,300. The value of lending also surged by 20.5% to £6.2bn, highlighting a growing trend among older homeowners to leverage their property wealth.

Drivers Behind the Surge in Later Life Borrowing

Several factors are contributing to the rise in later life mortgage activity. Firstly, the escalating cost of living is leaving many retirees with tighter budgets, prompting them to explore ways to release equity from their homes. This provides a practical solution to supplement their monthly income.

Secondly, soaring property prices, particularly in areas like London, have made it increasingly difficult for first-time buyers to enter the market. As a result, parents and grandparents are increasingly tapping into their home equity to help younger family members secure their first property.

Lastly, a growing number of homeowners who initially took out mortgages extending beyond retirement are now restructuring their borrowing. This trend is reflected in the 5.9% year-on-year increase in retirement interest-only (RIO) mortgages, with lending values rising by 24% to £31m.

Later Life Mortgages in the Wider Market

Later life borrowing continues to play a significant role in the broader mortgage market. Residential later life loans accounted for 7.8% of all residential loans advanced during Q2 2026. This proportion was even more pronounced in the buy-to-let sector, where later life borrowing made up 20.6% of all new loans.

Lifetime mortgage activity, however, remained relatively subdued. Although there was an 8% quarter-on-quarter increase, the number of new lifetime mortgages advanced during Q2 2026 was 1.7% lower than the same period in 2025, with lending totalling £490m.

David Forsdyke, head of later life lending at Knight Frank Finance, noted that the figures were partly influenced by the stamp duty changes in April 2025, which prompted many borrowers to bring forward their plans. He added, “The rise in borrowing costs over the past three years hasn’t dampened demand, highlighting the enduring appeal of later life borrowing.”

Rachel Springall, a finance commentator at Moneyfactscompare, emphasised the importance of later life lending for homeowners. She pointed out that the 13.4% year-on-year increase in new loans reflects a strong desire among older borrowers to access their property wealth, whether to support their retirement or assist younger family members.

As the later life mortgage market continues to evolve, homeowners may find it beneficial to explore their options carefully. With a range of products available, including RIO and lifetime mortgages, borrowers could consider seeking professional advice to determine the best solution for their financial needs.

item.title: Buyers return as housing market gathers momentum
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK housing market is showing signs of renewed activity as buyer interest rebounds following the traditional summer slowdown, according to the latest Zoopla House Price Index. Despite mortgage rates remaining significantly higher than at the start of the year, property searches have increased by 7% annually – the strongest growth since the spring rate rises. While agreed sales remain 6% below 2022 levels, analysts note the gap is beginning to narrow as more purchasers return to the market.

Affordability pressures reshape borrowing power

Higher interest rates continue to impact purchasing power, with average five-year fixed rates climbing from below 4% in January to around 4.8% currently. Zoopla estimates this has reduced typical borrowing capacity by approximately 9% – meaning a buyer who could previously secure £200,000 might now only access £182,000 for the same monthly repayment. To maintain their original borrowing level without increasing repayments, homeowners would need to contribute an additional £18,200 deposit on average.

Regional variations are pronounced, with London buyers facing the steepest climb – requiring £35,500 more for deposits compared to £10,200 in the North East. First-time buyers are particularly affected as they generally borrow higher loan-to-value ratios and often opt for longer mortgage terms, making them more sensitive to rate changes.

Search activity rises across all regions

Property searches have increased year-on-year in every UK region for the first time since August 2025, suggesting growing market confidence. The South East leads with an 8.9% annual rise in searches, followed closely by the East of England at 8.5%. Even the North West, with the smallest increase at 0.7%, shows positive movement. While these figures indicate strengthening demand, analysts caution that the translation into completed sales typically occurs with a time lag.

The supply side is also showing movement, with new property listings approaching last year’s levels. Total available stock sits 5% higher than in 2022, giving buyers more choice and potentially moderating price growth. Sellers are becoming more active too, with late summer traditionally bringing price adjustments as vendors prepare for the autumn market.

House price growth has slowed to 0.9% annually as the market adjusts to higher borrowing costs, down from 1.3% in June. With affordability constraints likely to persist, the coming months may see continued price sensitivity alongside gradual improvements in market activity.

item.title: Only 4% landlords seeking to expand
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research suggests just 4% of UK landlords currently plan to expand their property portfolios, with many citing increased taxation and regulatory burdens as key deterrents. The findings highlight a cautious approach amongst buy-to-let investors, with most preferring to maintain rather than grow their existing holdings.

Tax changes dampen landlord enthusiasm

Several recent tax reforms appear to be influencing landlords' investment decisions. Key changes include:

  • Reduction of mortgage interest tax relief, now fully phased out
  • The 3% stamp duty surcharge on additional properties
  • Capital gains tax allowances being halved in April 2023

These measures have significantly altered the financial landscape for property investors. Many landlords report their profit margins have narrowed considerably, making portfolio expansion less attractive than in previous years.

Regulatory pressures add to challenges

Alongside tax changes, landlords face an evolving regulatory environment that requires careful navigation. Recent and upcoming requirements include:

  • Stricter energy efficiency standards (EPC C rating proposed by 2028)
  • Renters' Reform Bill changes to tenancy agreements
  • Selective licensing schemes in many local authorities

Whilst these measures aim to improve rental standards, they also increase landlords' administrative burdens and potential costs. Some investors may be waiting for greater clarity on future regulations before committing to further purchases.

For those considering property investment, thorough research and professional financial advice remain essential. The current climate presents both challenges and opportunities, with location and property type becoming increasingly important factors in achieving sustainable returns.

item.title: Angela Rayner urged to U-turn on rent controls – legal experts respond
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner is under increasing pressure to reconsider her stance on rent controls, with a group of MPs urging the government to address affordability issues in the private rental sector. A letter, spearheaded by Labour MP Chris Hinchliff, has garnered support from 26 MPs, including members of Labour, the Green Party, and former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. The appeal calls for the introduction of rent controls to ease financial burdens on tenants. However, Rayner has previously dismissed the idea, citing concerns that such measures have not effectively reduced rents in other countries and highlighting the protections already offered by the Renters’ Rights Act.

The Debate Over Rent Controls

The government has firmly stated it has “no plans to introduce rent controls,” a position welcomed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS). The think tank has warned that rent controls could have unintended consequences, including a potential reduction in housing supply and lower property prices. Whilst existing tenants might benefit from capped rent increases in the short term, the IFS argues that such policies could discourage landlords from maintaining their investments in the rental market.

IFS economists Matthew Oulton and Tom Wernham pointed to international evidence suggesting that rent controls often lead to a decline in both the availability and quality of rental properties. “Rent controls can reduce the supply of rental homes and negatively impact property sale prices,” they noted. Whilst a decrease in house prices might assist some renters in transitioning to homeownership, many would still face barriers due to insufficient income or savings for a deposit.

Potential Impact on the Rental Market

Kristine Ng, partner at Morr & Co, echoed the IFS’s concerns, emphasising that rent controls could deter investment in the private rented sector. “Whilst tenants may gain short-term security, the long-term risks to housing supply are significant,” she said. Ng highlighted that landlords may opt to sell their properties if returns become too restricted, potentially shrinking the rental market further. This, in turn, could exacerbate the existing housing shortage and place additional strain on the sector.

The IFS analysis suggests that a wave of landlords selling properties could lead to falling house prices, which might benefit some renters. However, the broader implications, such as reduced rental availability and potential declines in property maintenance standards, raise concerns about the sustainability of such a policy.

As the debate continues, homeowners and renters alike may wish to stay informed about potential changes to housing policies and their implications for the property market.

item.title: Burnham faces pressure for major property tax overhaul
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is under growing pressure to reform the UK’s property tax system, with campaigners and economists proposing a shift to a proportional property tax (PPT). The suggested overhaul would replace council tax and stamp duty with an annual levy based on current property values, potentially lowering bills for some homeowners whilst increasing contributions from owners of higher-value homes.

What Would a Proportional Property Tax Involve?

Under proposals championed by groups like Fairer Share and supported by some Labour figures, a PPT would introduce an annual charge of 0.48% of a property’s market value. Additional rates could apply to second homes (0.96%) and properties owned by foreign nationals. This system might particularly affect homeowners in London and the South East, where property values are typically higher, whilst potentially reducing costs for those in lower-value areas.

Economists suggest the reforms could redistribute tax burdens more equitably. Michael Jacobs, former adviser to Gordon Brown and editor of a Compass policy collection, notes that many households might see reduced bills under PPT. However, the proposals could prove politically challenging, as Burnham has indicated major reforms aren’t currently a priority despite his past support for fairer property taxation principles.

Broader Proposals for Tax Reform

The PPT forms part of wider suggestions for rebalancing the UK’s tax system. Professor Ben Ansell of Oxford University, writing for the IPPR, proposes aligning capital gains tax with income tax rates and extending National Insurance contributions to older workers. These measures aim to address generational inequalities, where younger workers currently bear a disproportionate tax burden compared to those who’ve benefited from rising property wealth.

Critics argue that sudden changes could destabilise the housing market, whilst supporters highlight potential benefits: simplified administration, reduced upfront costs for first-time buyers (through stamp duty abolition), and a system where tax contributions better reflect property values. The Fairer Share campaign estimates London alone might contribute an additional £7.5bn annually under their model.

With housing affordability remaining a key issue, these proposals are likely to fuel ongoing debates about fair taxation. Homeowners may wish to monitor developments, as any future changes could significantly affect household finances across different regions and property brackets.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act drives more landlords into hands of letting agents
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research suggests private landlords are increasingly relying on letting agents to navigate the growing complexity of rental sector regulations. A survey by the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) reveals 66% of its members now use letting agents – the highest proportion recorded in at least two years. This shift comes as the sector prepares for further changes under the forthcoming Renters’ Rights Act.

Growing demand for professional management

The NRLA’s findings highlight how regulatory changes are reshaping landlord behaviour. With evolving tenancy laws and compliance requirements, many property owners appear to be opting for professional management services rather than handling tenancies themselves. The association notes this trend underlines the need for minimum education and training standards across the lettings industry.

However, tenant satisfaction data suggests room for improvement in agent-managed properties. Official figures show 73% of tenants with landlord-managed properties were satisfied with repairs, compared to just 59% in fully agent-managed homes. This disparity has prompted calls for better industry standards.

Calls for urgent regulatory reform

The NRLA is urging the government to accelerate plans for mandatory training requirements for letting agents, rather than waiting for a proposed consultation next year. Ben Beadle, NRLA chief executive, commented: “As the rental market becomes more complex, reliance on letting agents is only likely to grow further. Reforms to the agency sector should therefore go hand in hand with the wider changes to the rental market.”

While acknowledging that many agents provide excellent service, the association has expressed concerns about those lacking sufficient knowledge of legal responsibilities. Beadle added: “Minimum training standards would help ensure those working in the sector understand their responsibilities and can provide a consistently professional service.”

With two-thirds of rental properties now involving letting agents to some degree, these professional standards could become increasingly important for both landlords and tenants navigating the evolving private rental sector.

item.title: Property industry reacts to Zoopla House Price Index
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The latest Zoopla House Price Index indicates tentative signs of recovery in the UK property market, with buyer searches rising 7% annually despite ongoing affordability pressures. Industry experts caution that whilst activity is picking up after the summer lull, full market recovery remains constrained by higher mortgage costs and deposit requirements.

Autumn bounce expected as mortgage rates stabilise

Market analysts note that autumn typically brings increased housing activity, with this year's seasonal uplift potentially more pronounced than spring's modest recovery. Knight Frank's head of UK residential research observed that mortgage rates have stabilised, albeit approximately one percentage point higher than pre-2023 levels.

The relative absence of disruptive Budget speculation this summer has provided more stability for buyers considering their options. However, industry voices suggest that renewed political uncertainty or tax policy changes in the coming months could impact market momentum.

Affordability challenges persist for buyers

Whilst buyer interest shows signs of recovery, property professionals emphasise that affordability remains the primary market constraint. Compared to early 2023, households now face borrowing capacity reductions of around 9%, with first-time buyers particularly affected by the £18,200 higher deposits needed to maintain mortgage repayments at current rates.

Estate agents report growing buyer enquiries and search activity across all regions, though transaction volumes remain 6% below 2022 levels. The increased supply of available properties is providing buyers with more choice and helping moderate price growth, though regional variations mean market conditions differ significantly across the country.

  • Buyer searches up 7% year-on-year
  • Mortgage borrowing power down 9% from start of 2023
  • Sales agreed still 6% below last year's levels
  • First-time buyers needing £18,200 extra for deposits

Property professionals advise that local market knowledge will be crucial in the coming months, helping buyers understand realistic budgets and ensuring sellers price properties appropriately. Whilst the return of buyer demand is encouraging, experts agree that affordability constraints remain the key obstacle to a sustained market recovery.

item.title: House price growth shifts beyond the big cities
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals a striking shift in UK house price growth, with commuter towns now outperforming their neighbouring city centres. The trend, identified across all major urban areas analysed, suggests a growing preference for suburban living amidst changing affordability pressures.

London leads the commuter belt surge

The capital has seen the most dramatic divergence between urban and suburban property values. While London itself recorded a 3.7% annual price decline, surrounding commuter towns witnessed a 0.9% increase - creating a 4.6 percentage point gap. This suggests many buyers are prioritising more affordable locations within reasonable travelling distance of central London workplaces.

Cardiff displayed the second-largest discrepancy, with 6.7% growth in commuter areas compared to 2.9% in the city centre. Nottingham and Birmingham followed similar patterns, where modest city price declines contrasted with steady growth in their suburbs. Even traditionally resilient northern cities weren't immune to this trend, with Glasgow's commuter belt growth doubling the city's rate at 5% versus 2.5%.

Regional variations in the urban-suburban divide

The research examined 12 major UK cities, finding consistent but varying degrees of commuter belt outperformance:

  • Manchester: 0.5% city growth vs 2.7% in commuter areas
  • Sheffield and Newcastle: 1.9-2 percentage point gaps favouring suburbs
  • Liverpool and Leeds: Minimal differences under 0.5 points
  • Bristol: Just 1 percentage point separating city and commuter growth

Verona Frankish, CEO of Yopa which conducted the research, noted: "Higher mortgage rates have significantly impacted buyer affordability in recent years. While conditions have improved somewhat, purchasers are making more calculated decisions about location versus budget."

The analysis suggests that whilst the suburban premium exists nationwide, its intensity varies considerably by region. Homeowners considering a move might find better value in commuter towns, particularly around high-pressure markets like London. However, those in northern cities may find the price differentials less compelling when weighing against commuting costs.

As mortgage rates remain elevated compared to historic lows, this urban-to-suburban shift could persist. Borrowers seeking maximum space for their budget may continue favouring locations that balance accessibility with relative affordability.

item.title: Overlooked housing scheme could unlock hundreds of stalled developments
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A rarely used affordable housing scheme could help revive hundreds of stalled property developments across England, according to new research from Savills. The Discounted Market Sale (DMS) model may offer a solution when developers struggle to find housing associations to purchase affordable homes required under Section 106 agreements.

Alternative route for stalled developments

Traditional Section 106 agreements typically require developers to provide affordable housing, with housing associations purchasing these properties. However, recent financial pressures have led many associations to reduce their buying activity. Research from the Home Builders Federation reveals approximately 8,500 consented affordable homes lacked buyers as of October 2025, with over 700 sites experiencing delays or stalling completely.

The situation particularly affects smaller housebuilders, who often rely on project-specific financing and may need to secure affordable housing buyers before progressing developments. Savills suggests greater flexibility to convert stalled Section 106 packages to DMS arrangements could help unlock these projects without requiring additional public funding.

How Discounted Market Sales work

DMS properties, which include First Homes, are sold at least 20% below market value, with this discount remaining permanently attached to the property for future buyers. Crucially, unlike traditional affordable housing models, DMS doesn't require housing association involvement, potentially making developments more viable.

Despite its potential, DMS currently represents less than 4% of affordable housing delivery, averaging just 1,760 completions annually over the past decade. Savills' research, supported by several industry bodies, indicates this model could play a much larger role in addressing housing shortages.

Significant potential buyer demand

Savills' analysis reveals substantial untapped demand for DMS properties. Their estimates suggest approximately 530,000 private renting families with children could afford a three-bedroom DMS home with a 30% discount and 5% deposit – representing 34% of such households. Even at a 20% discount, around 350,000 families would potentially qualify.

The research illustrates this using a hypothetical £300,000 property. At a 30% discount (£210,000), buyers would need a household income of around £49,000 with a 5% deposit. This compares to the £63,000 typically required for the full market price, potentially opening homeownership to many more families.

While challenges remain in implementing DMS more widely, the research highlights its potential to help unblock stalled developments and improve access to homeownership. As the housing market continues to face affordability pressures, alternative models like DMS may play an increasingly important role in meeting the UK's housing needs.
